chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Muhammad and Ahmad, the two sons of al-Hasan, from their father, from Thalabah ibn Maymun, from Ma'mar ibn Yahya ibn Sam, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about what people narrate from the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) regarding certain matters of the private parts, which he did not command nor forbid for the general public, but only for himself and his offspring. I said, 'How can that be?' He said, 'A verse made them permissible, and another verse made them forbidden.' We said, 'Is it that one of them abrogated the other, or are both clear rulings that should be acted upon?' He said, 'He had already explained it to them when he forbade it for himself and his offspring.' We said, 'What prevented him from explaining that to the people?' He said, 'He feared that they would not obey.' And if the Commander of the Faithful had firmly established his position, he would have implemented the entire Book of Allah and all the truth.

key_terms.الفُرُوجِ: Private parts / Generality of the ruling

ai.seo_question: Why are the Imams permitted to marry two sisters while the general public is forbidden from doing so?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar elucidates the principle of 'Jam' al-Ukhtayn' (marrying two sisters simultaneously), distinguishing between the general prohibition for the public and the specific permission for the Ahl al-Bayt. It addresses the juristic debate between abrogation (naskh) and simultaneous applicability (hukm), concluding that the Imams restricted this divine permission to themselves to prevent public confusion and ensure obedience, fearing that exercising full authority openly might lead to rejection.
